tldr: Twenty paths, sorted by how long they take instead of how interesting they sound. Four are open to the license you already hold, four want six to twelve months, three are real builds. Pick the tier your runway can carry, then pick one path inside it.

blocks.text: Twenty-two threads in the forum corpus ask a version of the same question, and the question is rarely which career to choose. Most of them are asking what exists at all. One SLP wrote that she feels dumb looking at other jobs because she has no idea how anything works outside of speech, schools and therapy places. Another wrote that the only thing keeping her in the field was not knowing what else she could do. Both had already decided. What they were short of was a list.
The only thing preventing me from leaving the field is not knowing what else I can do as a career.
Sorted by time, because time is the thing you are short of

A list sorted by how interesting the jobs sound puts a role you could start in three weeks next to one that costs two years of evenings, and gives you no way to tell them apart. The map below is sorted by runway instead. The top tier hires you on the credential in your wallet. The middle tier wants some new vocabulary and one piece of proof. The bottom tier is a genuine build with the highest ceilings and the longest wait. Documented SLP transitions took six to fifteen months, and some ran a year and a half to two and a half years, so the tier you choose is mostly a question of what your bank account and your patience can carry.

blocks.text: The map

Two paths in the top tier are not covered in the next lesson, for different reasons. Rehab management sits there because it is usually an internal move: clinical or program manager first, director later, on a ladder you can already see from your desk. Clinical research coordination sits there because entry is fast and no new credential is required, and it carries the one warning on this whole map. Its band runs $48,000 to $72,000 against an SLP median of $97,870, so a pay cut is the expected outcome rather than a risk. Two documented SLPs used it as a first step and nothing else. One went from a CF year to a university study coordinator role in about eighteen months, then into pharma patient safety for $10,000 more base and a $5,000 bonus.

blocks.title: Telehealth is a bridge, and it is still clinical
blocks.text: Teletherapy is the most common half-exit in the corpus and it belongs in your plan as a way to drop hours, lose the commute and buy back evenings for a search. It is not on this map, because the work is clinical, the pay tracks clinical, and platform contracts often pay less than in person. The non-clinical door at Presence, eLuma, Global Teletherapy or VocoVision is a job at the platform, not a caseload on it.

items: Open the tier that matches your runway and ignore the other two for now.
Tap every card in that tier and read the catch before you read the salary.
Star the two you would still be curious about on a Wednesday in February.

takeaways: The map is sorted by runway, so you can compare a three-week move with a two-year build without pretending they are the same decision.
Documented transitions took six to fifteen months, with some running to two and a half years.
Read every band against the SLP median of $97,870, because that is the number your budget is built on.
Clinical research coordination is the one path where a pay cut is the expected outcome, and it works as a first step rather than a destination.
Telehealth is a bridge that buys you hours; it is still clinical work and is not on this map.

tldr: Four jobs hire you on the license you already hold: clinical liaison, utilization review, clinical educator at a device company, and case management. Bands run from $54,000 to $135,000, entry takes weeks rather than months, and each one has a catch worth knowing before you spend an evening applying.

blocks.text: These four are the shortest distance between your current badge and a non-clinical paycheck. No bootcamp, no portfolio, no certificate, no year of evenings. Clinical liaison gets called the number one non-clinical title for rehab professionals, and the reason is unglamorous: the job requires a clinician and you are one. The catch across all four has the same shape. You stay close to the system you are leaving, which is exactly what some people want and what other people resent by month four.
What each one actually is, and who hires for it

**Clinical or rehab liaison.** You work between a hospital and a rehab facility: reading charts to judge whether a patient is appropriate for your program, answering the case manager's questions, being the person the discharge planner calls at four on a Friday. The band is $84,000 to $135,000 and the clinical credential is sufficient on its own. Encompass Health, Select Medical and Lifepoint all hire for it. The catch is that you are still inside acute care most days, and part of the job is relationship selling even when the title never says so.

**Utilization review.** You read a request for care against the criteria that decide whether it gets paid, and you write the decision. It is remote-heavy, entry is fast, and the band is $80,000 to $88,000, quoted hourly at $37 to $62. State Disability Determination Services is a second door: one SLP took a $13,000 pay cut to walk through it for the mobility and a PSLF-qualifying employer, which is a real tradeoff rather than a hidden cost. The catch is the part nobody advertises. You are often the person saying no, and you are saying it to clinicians who sound like you did last year.
100% remote (a literal dream for me)

**Clinical educator or trainer at a device company.** You train clinicians, families and school teams on a device or platform you already know how to prescribe. Tobii Dynavox calls the role Learning Consultant and Glassdoor puts it at $78,000 to $116,000; PRC-Saltillo, Lingraphica and Passy-Muir hire the same profile. Every device you have set up, every protocol you have taught a teacher to run, every CF you have supervised belongs on that list, and most SLPs undersell it badly. The catch is travel, so find the percentage in the posting before you fall in love with the job.

**Case management.** You coordinate a patient's care across settings, insurers and discharge, which is the unbilled half of your week already. Medical case manager pay sits at $54,100 to $81,900 in the 25th to 75th band, with the best-paying sectors in government and public administration at around $82,600 median and insurance at around $80,500. Inpatient rehab systems advertise higher numbers, and many of those postings quietly say RN required.

blocks.title: Picture the Wednesday before you apply
blocks.text: All four of these keep you inside the system you are leaving, and that is the trade you are making. Picture an ordinary Wednesday in one of them: same building, same acronyms, same people, different badge, no caseload. If that reads as relief, this tier is your fastest way out and you should be applying this month. If it reads as a halfway house, spend your evenings on the later tiers and take the longer road on purpose.

items: Search "clinical liaison" and "utilization review" with your state, and read the first five postings end to end.
Count how many of them ask for a credential you already hold.
Save the two you would actually take, and note the travel percentage or the license line on each.

takeaways: Four jobs treat your clinical license as the whole qualification: liaison, utilization review, clinical educator and case management.
Liaison pays $84,000 to $135,000 at Encompass Health, Select Medical and Lifepoint, and part of it is relationship selling.
Utilization review is remote-heavy and fast to enter, and the job often means being the person who says no.
Clinical educator roles at Tobii Dynavox, PRC-Saltillo, Lingraphica and Passy-Muir run $78,000 to $116,000, and travel is the variable to check first.
Read the license line on case management postings, because many inpatient rehab roles require an RN.

tldr: Four clusters produce most of the documented SLP outcomes: customer success and implementation, project management, healthcare data, and content and marketing. The numbers those people reported were $115,000 to $120,000, a doubled salary, $20,000 more base, and one raise after five years of clinical work.

blocks.text: When I look at where SLPs have actually landed, rather than where career articles say they could, the same four clusters keep coming back. What follows is what those people reported about themselves: the salary, the months, the application count. Some of it is unflattering. The data analyst below sent more than five hundred applications over six months before an offer came, and she is the success story.

**Customer success, implementation and training.** Health-tech, SaaS and ed-tech companies need someone who can teach a clinician to use their product and then keep them using it, which is the job you have already done with every family who stopped practicing at home in March. The range is $75,000 to $120,000, and it has the best effort-to-odds ratio on the whole map. One medical SLP came out at $115,000 to $120,000 as a remote SaaS manager after SV Academy's free customer success bootcamp and a paid internship. At the speech-tech companies, Expressable, Presence, Tobii Dynavox, PRC-Saltillo, Lingraphica and Passy-Muir, your license is the credential rather than a nice extra. The vocabulary you have to pick up first is churn, onboarding and health scores.

**Project and program management.** A caseload is concurrent project management with worse tooling and no software license. This cluster has the most six-figure outcomes in the file: one SLP landed a six-figure IT project manager role after a fifteen-month transition and six interviews across three rounds, doubling their SLP salary; another was an associate PM inside a year; a third was at about $90,000 salaried eighteen months in, after being paid $38 to $48 an hour as a clinician. The Google project management certificate is free to start, the CAPM costs $175, the PMP costs $400 plus a $139 PMI membership, and your clinical coordination hours can legitimately count toward the PMP's experience requirement.
no one took me seriously with a CAPM
blocks.from: an SLP who moved into project management

blocks.text: **Healthcare data.** The entry point is healthcare organizations rather than big tech: hospital quality teams working falls data and discharge follow-up, behavioral health organizations, payers. The band is $70,000 to $105,000. One SLP with about ten years mostly in early intervention became a fully remote healthcare quality analyst at $20,000 more base than their best SLP year, after five hundred applications in six months, thirteen interview processes and four finals, self-taught with free and low-cost certificates and a five-project portfolio. Another did a one-year online master's while working and came in at the same salary as their last SLP job, $15,000 below their peak home-health year, with guaranteed annual raises and 85k+ after the entry level.

**Content and marketing.** Explaining a swallow study to a frightened spouse in words he can act on is the skill this cluster pays for, and the range runs $80,000 to $141,000. One SLP moved into corporate marketing after about a year of applications and wrote, "I actually got a raise and bonus this year, whereas in my 5 years in healthcare I was given a .35 cent raise." Another started freelance with a single $200 article on Upwork and now runs a micro-agency. Income is lumpy at the beginning, especially freelance, and the first year is the hardest part of this path.

blocks.text: The door you can get in is one title below the job you want

items: Customer success: implementation specialist or onboarding manager first, customer success manager after.
Project management: coordinator or associate project manager, most often inside a healthcare organization or a nonprofit.
Healthcare data: quality, reporting or operations analyst at a hospital or a behavioral health organization, and not a data scientist role at a tech company.
Content and marketing: one published piece explaining something clinical to a non-clinical reader, then a health-tech or ed-tech content role.
Freelance counts as a door in content and in data, and one $200 article is a legitimate first line on a portfolio.
Pick the cluster whose bad day you could live with, not the one whose good day sounds best.
Search LinkedIn for that entry title plus "CCC-SLP" and find three people who already made the move.
Save those three profiles. You will message them in lesson 2.9.

takeaways: Customer success and implementation has the best effort-to-odds ratio, and at speech-tech companies your license is the credential.
Project management holds the most six-figure outcomes in the file, and certificates only work alongside translated experience.
Healthcare data pays well and grinds hard: one documented offer took 500 applications over six months.
Content and marketing runs $80,000 to $141,000, and freelance is a real on-ramp that started at one $200 article.
In all four clusters, apply to the title one rung below the one you want.

tldr: Five paths pay above clinical work and cost you a year of evenings: clinical informatics, instructional design, UX research, software engineering and conversation design. What each one costs in months, and what the SLPs who finished were earning at the end.

blocks.text: Everything in this lesson costs time you do not currently have. You would be doing it after the last note is written, at five or eight hours a week, for somewhere between six months and two years, while still carrying a caseload. People do it anyway for the ceiling. BLS puts the SLP median at $97,870, and the top of this tier sits well above the top of clinical work.

**Clinical informatics and EHR analysis, six to eighteen months.** The band is $97,800 to $154,000. If you have been the superuser who fixes everyone's templates, you have been doing unpaid informatics for years. The most-read exit post in the whole corpus was this exact move: eight years in acute care and a skilled nursing facility, then a clinical analyst role at the same hospital system, hybrid, $10,000 more. The same post said, in capitals, that you do not need a secondary master's. The months go into getting into a sponsor-track junior analyst role, a go-live or activation support gig, or an implementation consulting firm such as Nordic or Tegria. CAHIMS through HIMSS is the one credential here you can buy for yourself, and it has no experience prerequisite.

**Instructional design, six to twelve months.** Therapy goals are learning objectives, session sequencing is scaffolding, progress monitoring is evaluation, and the range is $70,000 to $100,000. The cost is a portfolio: three to five samples built in Articulate Storyline 360 or Rise, each with a short write-up of your process. Spec work is fully acceptable, so you can build every sample from trainings you have already delivered to colleagues. No degree and no certificate is required, and the $3,000 certificate is the most common way SLPs waste money on this path. Learn the vocabulary instead: ADDIE, Kirkpatrick levels, Mayer's principles, andragogy. The field got more crowded with the wave of teachers making the same move.

**UX research, twelve to twenty-four months.** Healthtech UX research runs $67,000 to $154,000 and is the realistic niche for someone with your background, because clinical fluency is the part most candidates cannot fake. The cost is two to four deep case studies, and the standard for those is higher than it looks.
One honest case study including the wrong turns is worth more than six polished AI case studies.

**Software engineering, one to two years of self-teaching.** Two SLPs in the file finished it. One went from two part-time jobs, $26 an hour in a skilled nursing facility and $34 an hour at a hospital, to $80,000 starting and $93,000 after two years, using free online courses; a recruiter found her on LinkedIn. The other reached $96,000 self-taught. This is the longest runway on the map and the least forgiving of a stop-start schedule, which is worth saying plainly if your current week already has nothing left in it.

**Conversation design, about twelve months.** Writing what a voice assistant or a chatbot says, and how it recovers when a person says something unexpected, is pragmatics with a deployment pipeline. Glassdoor puts conversational designer at $68,000 to $101,800 with an average of $82,700, and the IT-sector median total pay at $96,900; postings using the conversation designer title average lower, around $63,000. It is a small field, and most of the roles sit inside big tech and consultancies such as Amazon, Meta and Accenture, so the search is national even when the work is remote.

one self-taught SLP software engineer, starting pay and after two years

blocks.title: Count the cost in months, using your worst week
blocks.text: Six to eighteen months for informatics, six to twelve for instructional design, twelve to twenty-four for UX and software. Pick the number of hours a week you can give it on a bad week rather than a good one, and do the multiplication before you pay for anything. If the answer runs past the runway you set in Module 0, take a fast-tier job first and build this from inside it, on a salary, with your evenings back.

items: Pick one path from this lesson and write down the hours a week you can give it in a bad week.
Find its first free step: one Rise module, the CAHIMS outline, one free course lesson, one posting's required tool.
Do that first step this week and notice whether you resent it. That reaction is the cheapest data you will get.

takeaways: This tier buys a higher ceiling with evenings, and the honest unit of cost is months rather than dollars.
Clinical informatics pays $97,800 to $154,000, and the documented move was internal: superuser to analyst at the same hospital system.
Instructional design is decided by a portfolio of three to five Storyline or Rise samples, and spec work counts.
Software engineering took one to two years for both documented SLPs, ending at $93,000 and $96,000.
Before you commit, multiply your worst-week hours by the months, and compare that against the runway you set in Module 0.

tldr: Three claims circulate in SLP forums that will cost you money or a year: that you can buy an Epic certification, that medical science liaison is a realistic pivot, and that UX research is wide open. Each is wrong in a specific way, and each has a real route sitting behind it.

blocks.text: Every one of these three claims has a product attached to it. A course that promises Epic certification. A certificate that promises to make you a medical science liaison. A bootcamp that promises a UX research career. The claim is what gets repeated in threads, and the route behind it is what actually hires people.
Epic certification cannot be bought, only sponsored

Epic does not sell certification to individuals. It happens through an employer who sponsors you and pays for the training, so anyone selling you an Epic cert is selling you something else with that word on the label. The route that works is a sponsor-track junior analyst role, a go-live or activation support gig, or an implementation consulting firm such as Nordic or Tegria, all of which hire clinically credible people and train them into the software. If you want a credential you can buy for yourself, CAHIMS from HIMSS was designed for career changers and has no experience prerequisite. One SLP in the file became an Epic application analyst, and the most-read forum version of the move was internal, from the clinical floor of a hospital system into that system's own analyst team. Your ammunition is superuser work, template building and documentation-workflow expertise, which is precisely what a sponsor is looking for.
Medical science liaison is doctorate-gated

MSL roles are effectively gated behind a PhD, PharmD or MD. A clinical master's plus a certificate will not clear that gate, and the certificate industry around MSL exists largely to sell that hope to people holding clinical master's degrees. The accessible cousin is clinical or rehab liaison at $84,000 to $135,000, where your credential is sufficient and entry takes weeks. If it is specifically the pharma side you want, the documented route runs through clinical research: CF year to university study coordinator in about eighteen months, then pharma patient safety for $10,000 more base and a $5,000 bonus, then $15,000 more eighteen months after that.
UX research is oversaturated, and its niche is not

Graduate output in UX grew about 35% in five years while openings stayed flat, which is why the field reads as open in blog posts and closed in your inbox. Mostly aspirational is the honest description of SLP to UX research in the file: one documented story, a rehab director who went through a bootcamp. If you still want it, the route is the healthtech niche at $67,000 to $154,000, where your clinical fluency is a genuine advantage, and the thing that decides it is two to four deep case studies with the wrong turns left in. Conversation design and instructional design sit next door, are less crowded, and use most of the same muscles.

blocks.title: The twenty-minute check before you buy anything
blocks.text: All three of these follow one shape: a real job, a real salary band, and a gate that the person selling the shortcut leaves out. Before you pay for a credential, find it in three live postings and message two people who hold the job to ask what their employer actually required. One transitioner in the file spent $220 on a résumé writer and $480 on a career coach, then a teacher-transition program, before the thing that finally worked. Twenty minutes of checking would have bought them a better first guess.

items: Name the credential you have been tempted to buy.
Find three live postings for the job and count how many of them name it.
Message two people who hold the job and ask what their employer actually required. Spend nothing until both answers agree.

takeaways: Epic certification comes only through employer sponsorship; sponsor-track analyst roles, go-live gigs and firms like Nordic or Tegria are the way in, and CAHIMS is the credential you can buy yourself.
Medical science liaison is doctorate-gated, and clinical liaison at $84,000 to $135,000 is the accessible cousin.
UX research grew 35% more graduates in five years against flat openings, so the healthtech niche and two to four deep case studies are the only realistic route.
Each of these three myths has a product attached, which is why the myth keeps circulating.
Check any credential against three live postings and two people who hold the job before you spend a dollar.

tldr: Twenty paths is more than anyone can hold, and holding all of them is how people stay stuck for a year. The Pivot Report reads your actual résumé and returns a readiness profile, the stage you are in, three paths with entry doors, and a thirty-day plan. It is included, it takes about four minutes, and its whole job is to get you down to one.

blocks.text: Something predictable happens around this point in the module. You have read the map, you can name six paths, and you are further from a decision than you were in week one. Twenty options do that to a tired brain. A burnt-out brain in particular, which one SLP described as struggling with executive function at exactly the moment a career change demands it.
It's so frustrating not knowing how to start.
What the report does with your résumé

items: A readiness profile, one of four: depleted expert, quiet researcher, restless builder, ready leaper. Each comes with the trap that profile falls into and the strength it underrates.
The stage you are actually in, tied to your own answers rather than guessed, with the one thing to focus on now and the one thing you are allowed to ignore.
Your top three paths, each with why your specific experience fits, a range, a timeline in months, the entry door, and one first move.
A week-by-week thirty-day plan, sized for someone working full time with a caseload.
Outreach templates written in your own voice, with the honest reply rate attached to them.

blocks.text: What readiness means, and what it does not

The profile describes how you are approaching the change and makes no claim about whether you are good enough. A depleted expert needs a recovery-paced plan and cannot see their own competence from where they are standing. A quiet researcher has been reading and lurking for months and needs permission more than information. A restless builder has energy, four tabs open and no single target. A ready leaper wants tactics and no more reassurance. None of these is a grade. The useful line in each one is the watch-out, because the trap it names is usually something you have already done twice this year.

Read the three paths in order and notice which one you argue with, because that reaction is data. The report ranks on the evidence in your résumé, which is a different thing from what you want. If it puts clinical informatics first on the strength of an EMR rollout you barely remember, and you know you never want to open a chart again, write that down and take the second one. Choosing on purpose beats being ranked.

blocks.title: One path, and the other nineteen keep
blocks.text: Pick one path to carry through Modules 3, 4 and 5. Everything after this works better narrow: one résumé translated for one target, one proof artifact, one set of conversations. The other paths do not expire. People who changed target at week six still got there, and nobody got there holding six at once.

items: Build the report and read it once, straight through, without stopping to argue.
Write one sentence: "I am aiming at [path], and I will know by [date] whether it fits."
Put that sentence somewhere you will see it, and put the report in the same folder as your résumé.

takeaways: Twenty options is a decision trap, and the fix is committing to one path rather than reading a twenty-first article.
The report reads your real résumé and returns a readiness profile, your stage, three paths with entry doors, and a thirty-day plan.
The readiness profile describes your approach to the change, and the watch-out line is its most useful sentence.
It ranks paths on the evidence in your résumé, so disagreeing with it in writing is a legitimate way to choose.
One path carries through the next three modules; the other nineteen are still there if you change your mind.

tldr: Three live postings, read side by side, tell you more about a job than any article about it. The requirements that appear in all three are the actual job. Everything else is one company's wish list, and the gap between them is your plan for Module 4.

blocks.text: The most common question under every exit post in the corpus is some version of what the job actually is. "What does a project manager actually do?" "What does day to day look like as a clinical analyst? First i'm hearing about it." A job posting answers that question for free, today, in the employer's own words, and almost nobody sits down and reads three of them in a row.
Could you explain what you do in layman's terms?
Read three at once, in one document

items: Open three live postings for the same title and paste all three into one document.
Underline every requirement that appears in all three. That overlap is the job.
Mark each underlined line you already have evidence for, from a caseload, an EMR rollout, a supervision year or a program you built.
List what is left over. That is your gap list, and it is usually shorter than you feared.
Copy the exact words the postings use for the things you can already do. You will mirror that vocabulary in Module 3.

blocks.text: What to read that is not in the requirements

items: Title variants: implementation specialist, onboarding manager and customer success manager are three rungs of one ladder, and the first two hire career changers.
The knockout questions on the application form, which are the real filter, rather than the ranking software everyone worries about.
The travel percentage, which decides whether a clinical educator role fits your life at all.
The license line, because many case management postings quietly require an RN.
How the money splits in a sales or clinical specialist posting, since base and commission are two different promises.
Who the role reports to, which tells you whether you would be the only clinician in the room.

blocks.text: Applications sent in the first day or two of a posting are the ones that reliably get seen, so treat this week's reading as research and not as a submission deadline. You apply in Module 3, with a résumé that uses the vocabulary you are collecting now. If a posting shows up this week that you would take tomorrow, save it with the date and move on. A translated résumé sent fast beats an untranslated one sent faster.

Three postings takes about forty minutes at a kitchen table. Set that against the months of reading that most people in the corpus describe before they do anything, and it is the cheapest hour in this module. It also gives you something to say in lesson 2.9, because a message that quotes a real posting reads nothing like a message from someone browsing.

items: Read three postings for your top path and three for your second.
Write the gap list for both on one page.
Circle the gap that shows up in both lists. That is the proof artifact you build in Module 4.

takeaways: The requirements appearing in all three postings are the real job; everything else is one company's wish list.
Mark the lines you already have evidence for, and what is left is your gap list.
Copy the postings' exact vocabulary now, because Module 3 rewrites your résumé in those words.
Read past the requirements for travel percentage, the license line, the commission split and the knockout questions.
The gap that appears on both of your lists is the artifact to build in Module 4.

tldr: The message that gets answered is short, specific, and asks for fifteen minutes about their path with no job attached. About one in four asks never gets a reply, which is a volume problem rather than a verdict. Three templates below: the first message, the single follow-up, and the thank-you that keeps the door open.

blocks.text: Referrals decide most of the successful transitions in the file, and generic online applications through Indeed and LinkedIn without a referral is what fails. The forum threads already suspect this. Under one exit post, somebody asked whether the writer had found the job through network connections or just by submitting a résumé, and some version of that question sits under most of them.
Did you find the new position through network connections or just by submitting your resume?

The ask that works is small. Fifteen minutes, about how they got in, with no job attached to it. Expect roughly one in four of these to go unanswered, which means three messages is usually two conversations. Nobody in the corpus reported being annoyed by a polite ask from an SLP. What they reported, repeatedly, was being asked for their actual résumé, more than twenty times under a single post, and mostly saying yes.

Four things make a first message answerable. You name the specific move they made, so it is obvious you are writing to them and not to forty people. You ask for a fixed, small amount of time. You attach no job ask, which removes the awkwardness of them having to say no to something they cannot give you. And you make it easy to decline, which is the part most people leave out and the part that makes a stranger feel safe replying at all.

blocks.title: The first message (LinkedIn or email, under 90 words)
blocks.text:
Hi [Name], I'm an SLP in [setting] and I'm looking at [target title] roles. I found you because you made the same move, and I'd rather ask you than read another article about it.

Would you be up for 15 minutes in the next couple of weeks? I mostly want to know how you got the first one and what you'd do differently. No job ask, I promise.

Either way, thank you for putting your path somewhere someone like me could find it.

[Your name]

One follow-up, seven to ten days later, and then you stop. Silence is almost always a full inbox and a bad Tuesday. A second follow-up converts almost nobody and costs you the option of asking again in six months, when you have something new to say. Keep it to two sentences and offer a smaller way to say yes.

blocks.title: The follow-up, once, seven to ten days later
blocks.text:
Hi [Name], floating this back up in case it got buried.

Still would love 15 minutes on how you got into [target title]. If a call is too much, I'd happily take two sentences by message instead: what surprised you most in your first three months?

Thank you either way. [Your name]

items: What did you actually do yesterday? Ask for the day, not the job description.
What did your employer require, and what did they ignore on your résumé?
Which part of clinical work turned out to be the most useful, and which part did you have to unlearn?
What would you do differently if you were starting this month?
Who else should I be talking to? This is the only question that turns a conversation into an introduction, so never skip it.

blocks.title: The thank-you, same day
blocks.text:
[Name], thank you for the time. The thing I'm taking away is [one specific sentence they said, in their words].

I'm going to [the one concrete thing you'll do because of it] in the next two weeks, and I'll let you know how it lands. If [person they mentioned] would be open to the same 15 minutes, I'd be grateful for an introduction whenever it's convenient.

Thank you again. [Your name]

Send the thank-you the same day, then actually do the thing you said you would do, and tell them two weeks later that you did it. That second note is what turns a stranger into someone who forwards your résumé to a hiring manager, and it is the entire referral mechanism, built out of two emails and one kept promise. Fill your setting, your target title and your name into all three templates tonight, and leave the [Name] blanks empty. You fill those in the next lesson.

takeaways: Referrals decide most documented transitions, and applications sent without one are what fails.
The ask is fifteen minutes about their path with no job attached, and about one in four goes unanswered.
A first message works when it names their specific move, asks for a fixed small amount of time, and makes it easy to decline.
Follow up once, seven to ten days later, then stop.
"Who else should I be talking to?" is the question that turns a conversation into an introduction.

tldr: Three messages, twenty minutes, tonight. About one in four gets no answer, so three sent is usually two conversations, and one conversation is worth more than another week of reading.

blocks.text: Everything in this module so far has been reading. This is the first step that involves another person, and it is the one people postpone for months. I put it off myself and called it research, which is what research becomes once you already know the answer.

Three people, and they do not all have to be strangers. In order of value: an SLP who now holds the title you want, because they have already done the exact translation you are attempting; anyone who holds that title from any background, because they know what their employer actually required; and someone at a company on your list, because a name inside beats a posting outside. Search LinkedIn for your target title plus "CCC-SLP" and the first page will surprise you. The companies directory holds 120 employers that have hired for these roles, and the deep-dive tool in lesson 2.7 already listed the ones matching your path.
Why three, and why tonight

Three is a volume decision. About one in four of these asks gets no answer at all, so one message is a coin flip and three is a near-certainty of at least one real conversation. Sending three at once also stops you reading a single silence as a verdict on you, which is what ends most outreach after message one. Do it tonight, in one sitting, with the templates already filled in, because a tired brain will not do this on a Thursday three weeks from now.

blocks.title: Do not ask for a job in the first message
blocks.text: The ask is fifteen minutes about their path. A job ask puts a stranger in the position of saying no to something they cannot give you, and it is the most common reason these messages go unanswered. The referral comes later, at the end of a good conversation, when you ask who else you should be talking to.

What comes back is rarely a job, and that is fine. What comes back is a description of an ordinary Tuesday, the name of the credential their employer actually cared about, a posting that is not public yet, or a second name. Any one of those is worth more than another week of reading, and by Module 4 you will need one of these people to vouch for you.
